Character card entries, ideoligion rows, transfer lists, the quests tab, pawn summaries in the work and animal tables, meme details, and stat entries all read their explanatory text with the row it belongs to. Installed mods get the same treatment. Bare icons are no longer silent either, and labels cut short by a narrow column now read in full.
  • Anyone watching your screen can now follow along. The map cursor is drawn as a highlighted cell, every screen outlines the row or cell you are on and scrolls it into view, keyboard placement draws the same preview a mouse drag shows, targeting draws its range circle, and the research tree scrolls to the project you are reading. Since dialogs and menus are now the game's real windows, a sighted person can also just use the mouse alongside you.
  • The trade window now has two views, and Ctrl+Tab switches between them on the open window with your choice remembered. The classic view is the three-list design that has always been here, holding the trader's goods, the pending deal with its running balance, and your goods, moved between with Left and Right. The new one is a table view laid out the way the game itself draws the trade screen. Some testers found the table harder to get around, so classic is still the default, and there is a Default Trade View setting in Options. Both views share the same reading and editing: each row reads its name, what you have queued, both prices with the game's own good-deal and bad-deal wording, and the running total, and Enter opens the quantity chooser, where Up and Down step by one, Shift or Ctrl with the arrows step by ten or a hundred, and typing a number sets the amount.
  • A new experimental mouse mode, off by default in Options. With hover speech on, whatever the pointer moves onto is read: controls and their tooltips, map cells with their terrain sounds, letters, the colonist bar, and the command bar. Clicking says what got selected, and drags speak their size and result. Two keys bridge the pointer and the cursor: Alt+J sends the pointer to your cursor, and Alt+Shift+J pulls your cursor to whatever the pointer is on. Alt+Shift+K makes the pointer follow the cursor continuously, and Alt+Shift+M toggles hover speech. Pointer movement is well tested on macOS and newly available on Windows and X11 Linux.
  • A new Configure Spoken Announcements screen, the top item in Options under RimWorld Access. Every part of an announcement (name, shortcut, control type, control state, position, tree level, description, hints) can be switched off or reordered. Control type and state are separate parts, so you can hear the type like "checkbox" without the state like "checked", or reorder them independently. You hear each change as you make it, and Restore Defaults puts everything back. It is now the one place the announcement format lives, and every screen follows it right away.
  • Five new complete translations: French, Turkish, Castilian Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, and European Portuguese. Each covers every interface string and the in-game documentation, using the game's own official wording for that language. Simplified Chinese, Russian, Latin American Spanish, and Ukrainian are complete again and cover everything new in this release.
  • Developer mode is now fully accessible. The debug action menu, debug output tables, the log window with full messages and stack traces, the inspector, tweak values, the def editor, and the map and world debug tools all read and work, with typeahead search throughout. With dev mode on, the mod also reads the extra detail sighted developers see, like exact hediff severities and world tile IDs.
  • New: a combat autopilot for drafted pawns. Assign a combat policy and the pawn fights on its own; leave it on None and it only follows your direct orders. Abilities can be autocast, all at once or one at a time. A Pause checkbox suspends everything without losing the setup, and the checkboxes apply to your whole selection at once. What the autopilot is doing becomes the pawn's job, so cycling colonists or arrowing over a pawn tells you the tactic: "moving to cover", "holding position and firing", "attacking Raider". It is entirely optional, and a settings switch removes it completely. Drafted mechanoids, modded draftable animals, and Vehicle Framework vehicles are all supported.
  • Combat policies are named sets of fighting behaviors, one checkbox each, managed in a real policy window just like drug or food policies. Assign them from the combat policy column in the Assign tab, or from the Animals and Mechs tabs for draftable pawns. Three presets ship: Full control, Fight nearby, and Stay safe. Every choice has a plain-language tooltip saying exactly what it turns on. Optional safety behaviors are part of a policy: keeping distance from melee attackers, falling back when badly hurt, and running clear of explosives. Retreats say why they happened, for example "badly hurt, falling back to 120, 45".
  • Drafted pawns take three new kinds of order. Engage target sends a pawn after one specific enemy until it is down, available as a command or from the right-click menu on anything attackable. Search and destroy sends a pawn hunting hostiles on its own. Patrol (Shift+T) picks an area for a pawn to walk a beat in, stopping to fight anything that comes into range. A new Mark for attack designator on the Orders tab marks single targets or sweeps whole areas, and pawns on search and destroy go for marked targets first. Every autopilot command has a rebindable shortcut behind Shift, and each wears its own icon so they are easy to tell apart on screen.
  • Drafted pawns can hunt. A Hunt animals checkbox on any drafted pawn makes it chase and kill wild animals the way sighted players hunt with drafted colonists. Hunting policies, managed like food and drug policies, decide which animals each pawn may go after, with a revenge-chance slider and a species filter. Two presets ship: Safe game and Any animal. Hunting stands down while any hostile threat is on the map.
  • Pawn dialogue from Interaction Bubbles and RimTalk is now narrated as it happens, including lines you type as your colony's persona. Settings control whether it is announced, whether vanilla interactions count, and at what priority. A new Dialogue Log screen, on F12 when either mod is installed, lists every recorded line newest first and carries the related controls.
  • Placing a building tells you much more. The notes the game draws beside the cursor are spoken as they change: which facilities the building would link to, how far the nearest one of its kind is, and substructure footprints. Areas with their own requirements, like the moving water a water mill needs, are described with size, direction, and whether the current spot will do. A temporary Placement spots scanner category lists the nearest positions where the building actually fits, closest first, and Home jumps you there with the rotation already set. In god mode, placement warns before destroying whatever is already there.
  • The mod now tells you when it has updated. A What's New reader on the main menu presents the release notes you have not read yet, oldest first, with a link to the full changelog. The reader and the website are linked from the main menu and the pause menu, and a setting turns the popup off.
  • The History tab is now covered in full, including the Graph page. Every recorder in every graph group (wealth, population, colonist mood, and any a mod adds) is summarized with its current value, range, and trend over the chosen dates, with a day-by-day drill-in. The Messages page now includes quest dialogs, caravan encounters, and narrative entries alongside letters.
  • The credits screen, including the victory text after launching the ship or reaching any other ending, is now fully readable. It reads as one document with jumps between sections, the visible scroll follows your position, and skipping says so instead of just going quiet.
  • Commands reach further. The inspection tree gained a Gizmos node carrying the same commands the G menu offers, each read as the control it really is, with disabled ones kept in the list along with the game's reason. Marking commands like Chop Wood, Mine, or Hunt now say how many things they marked. Enter works with Shift, Ctrl, or Alt held, for tools that change under modifier keys, and a tool's extra options open on the right bracket key.
  • The research detail view now shows everything the game shows: tech level and exact progress, required benches, facilities, and techprints as their own rows with info cards, the unlocks the game itself computes, which mod or expansion the project comes from, and the dev-mode finish and techprint actions.
  • Dozens of controls that used to be mouse-only now work from the keyboard. Among them: the auto-refuel checkbox on fuel gizmos, renouncing a royal title, the ideoligion hair, beard, and tattoo style editors, the xenotype icon picker, custom xenotypes in the starting-pawn picker, the mechanitor recharge threshold, quest reward preferences, the Work table's copy and paste column, the Mods screen's Workshop upload button, the saved preferred names list, and info cards for filter items, drug policies, and starting-pawn possessions.
  • Gene rows now say what the game's own hover text says about conflicts. When several genes compete for the same slot, the one that applies reads as "active" and the others name the gene suppressing them, so a list of four skin colors no longer sounds like four equal choices. Genes the game picks between at random name the whole pool. A pawn's own gene rows now read complexity, metabolic efficiency, and the description too.
  • Two new sounds. Moving the keyboard cursor plays the game's own soft mouseover click, because I love the game's UI sounds. And there is now, finally, a sound for when menus and screens wrap.
  • The flight recorder now ships in the release build, for your bug reports. (There won't be any, of course, because RimWorld Access is perfect!) Press Alt (Option on a Mac) plus the game's screenshot key (F10 by default) to start recording from anywhere, and press it again to stop. It captures what the mod heard and said, never anything outside the game. When you stop, a dialog tells you where the file was saved with a button to open the folder. Attach that file to a bug report and we can see your exact session.
  • Typeahead search in tables now finds columns, not just rows. Typing a column name, like "tame" in the Animals tab or a work type in the work table, moves you to that column and keeps you on the row you were on. Cell contents are searchable too, ranked below column and row names, so you can type a master's name and land on the cell that holds it.
  • The game's color pickers, for allowed-area colors and lamp glow, are now full keyboard screens: a palette of named colors with Default and Darklight rows, Hue and Saturation rows standing in for the color wheel, a readback of the current and old color, and the real Cancel and Accept buttons. Shift+Enter accepts.
  • Ctrl+C copies a colonist's work priorities and Ctrl+V pastes them onto another, in both the focused view and the table view.
  • RimWorld Access can keep the game paused when it matters. New games start paused and quiet, opening the research screen from a finished-research popup stays paused, and the game stays paused after you close a trade. Each is a setting you can switch off.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Navigation is consistent within each kind of screen now, instead of being reinvented screen by screen. Several shapes remain, because the game's own interface has several: trees, tables, screens whose sections you move between with Left and Right, and screens whose sections you move between with Tab. What is shared is everything inside them. Every row announces the same way, in the order you choose. Checkboxes say checked or not checked and toggle with Space or Enter, dropdowns open on Enter, sliders and steppers adjust with Left and Right and accept a typed value, radio buttons select as you arrow onto them, tables read cell by cell under sortable headers, and disabled controls stay in the list and say why.
  • You can always reach a screen's buttons. The game's own toolbar is now shown on every screen and Tab walks every button on it, so you should not end up stranded on a screen not knowing which key moves you forward. Shift+Enter presses the screen's next button from anywhere on it, whether that is Generate, Save, Done, or Accept. Enter on something that is not an interactive control names the button a second Enter would press, so you hear the consequence before committing to it.
  • Dialogs and menus are now the game's real windows instead of invisible keyboard overlays. Confirmations, letters and choice dialogs, order menus, renaming, the options screen, save and load, the schedule table, bed assignment, and the pause menu all appear on screen exactly as the game draws them, with a highlight following your cursor. Because they are the real thing, they pause the game by the game's rules, play its own sounds, and take mouse clicks alongside the keys.
  • Typeahead search is stronger everywhere. Multi-word queries work: pressing Space extends the search, so "left arm" finds the Left arm row, and shorthand like "ga pi" reaches gas pipe (thanks to Rashad's OniAccess mod for the pattern). Ranking favors the row you actually named, and a search reaches everything on screen including section headers and toolbar buttons. Home and End jump between matches without ending the search. Enter activates what the search found; Shift+Enter lands on it without activating, for when you want to hear where you are first.
  • Map scanner improvements. Cycling categories now only recalculates the one you land on, so it is much faster on big or busy maps. Vehicles and other controllable units get their own category and their own section of the colonist bar. Things are sorted by the game's own data rather than by their label text, so modded races, debris, and buildings file correctly in every language. The scanner also keeps working while you pick a transport pod or shuttle landing spot. A category now reads its name and a real count, followed straight away by its first item: a group of twelve steel stacks counts as twelve, and destroyed things are not counted. Auto-jump is now a saved setting, so it stays on between sessions.
  • Wherever the mod used to keep its own hand-written copy of something, it now reads the game's live data instead: the main menu, material menus, order menus, table columns, tab lists, scenario parts, and more. In practice this means content added by mods or by future game updates shows up automatically, in the same order sighted players see it, without waiting for RimWorld Access to catch up.
  • Far fewer "tab" announcements. Opening a screen speaks the focused item directly, pressing Tab speaks the section's name and where you landed, and the word "tab" is now reserved for real tab strips, the way NVDA treats them. The optional count on entry says "2 sections" instead of "2 tabs". On a screen with only one section, Tab does nothing rather than re-announcing everything. Screens whose section names already tell you where you are, like the work tab's priority levels, no longer add "section 2 of 5" after them.
  • Ctrl and an arrow key now has four jump modes instead of two, cycled with Shift and Up or Down. Preset distance is unchanged. The old "Adjacent to wall" is now Impassable, and Structure jumps to the next tile whose building differs, so a run of marble wall or a stretch of sand crosses in one press. A jump also says how many tiles it covered.
  • Target sliders on command buttons now adjust with Left and Right directly in the command menu, with Shift for bigger steps, and each press applies immediately. The separate right-bracket adjustment mode is gone. Enter on these buttons still does what it always did. While the command menu is open, arrow keys belong to the menu alone and no longer move the map cursor underneath.
  • Arrow keys that run into an edge now play a short tone instead of re-reading the row you were already on, anywhere navigation does not wrap. This covers rows, table columns, toolbar buttons, tree views, command menus, the colonist bar, and the work tab in both its views.
  • Rename dialogs now submit when you press Enter after typing the new name, matching how the game behaves for sighted players. Shift+Enter also presses OK from anywhere in the dialog, and Escape still closes without renaming. Enter now expands and collapses read-only tree branches too, such as scenario parts and detail sections, instead of only re-reading them.
  • Manage Areas is now the game's real dialog everywhere: the Animals, Mechs, and Schedule area pickers, the per-pawn area menu, and the architect area tools all open it. It reads as a table with one row per area and one column per control: color, expand, shrink, invert, rename, copy, and delete, each announced as the button it is. Inverting an area now reports the resulting size instead of the vague "All cells toggled".
  • The learning helper got a round of work. It now opens with ? from any screen, including every world-generation step and while configuring an ideoligion, and Escape dismisses it. Its lesson-mode control is now a "Show all lessons" checkbox you flip with Space or Enter, matching the game's own plus/minus toggle, instead of a dropdown you had to open. Escape from a lesson's Mark Learned button now returns to the lesson list rather than closing the helper, and a lesson no longer marks itself finished and drops off the list the moment you reach its last line; it leaves the active list only once you step back to the lesson list.
  • The ideoligion appearance editor now behaves like every other tree in the mod. Category rows like Minimal or Punk announce as expandable tree items, individual styles as combo boxes, Left on a style collapses its category, and the tree respects your submenu navigation setting.
  • Arrowing down onto the buttons at the bottom of a reader screen, such as a letter, a quest, or the learning helper, no longer plays the tab-switch sound or announces a new section. The buttons read as a continuation of the text above them, so the whole thing feels like one strip. Tab still treats them as their own section where a screen offers that.
  • The main menu's Tutorial button is now hidden for keyboard users, since RimWorld's built-in tutorial depends on mouse-only, exact-placement steps a screen reader cannot follow.
  • Smaller changes: skill names are capitalized wherever they are read, matching the game; leaving placement mode with nothing pending says "Exited placement mode" rather than "Placement cancelled", making clear that confirmed work is kept; message and confirmation dialogs no longer prefix their text with the word "Description", and no longer announce "Dialog opened" first; menu rows that toggle something are now real checkboxes that keep the menu open; right-click and pop-up menus share the full search grammar; the Anomaly playstyle choices select on arrival like every other radio group; the storyteller page opens on the game's own fallback difficulty; and the flight recorder's saved-recording dialog is one clean button strip.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • The text panels the mod used to draw over the screen are gone: the world map information box, the landing-site panels, and the placement instruction box. The game's own highlights and windows carry that information now, and nothing is spoken any differently.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Speech no longer goes silent on Windows. Machines with AVX-512 processors were rejecting any announcement containing a non-ASCII character, so an accented letter, a curly apostrophe, or CJK text produced silence while plain English spoke normally. Announcements carrying stray invisible characters from mod content were dropped outright. Both are fixed, and any remaining speech failure now logs the exact text so it can be diagnosed from your log file.
  • Actions now go through the game's own rules everywhere, closing a long list of cases where this mod could do something the game would refuse, or skip a warning it would show. Among them: drafting respects downed pawns and mech overseer range; taming and slaughter show their bond, faction, and veneration confirmations; surgeries respect availability and speak the game's reason when refused; caravan equipping shows the persona weapon warning; accepting a quest shows the royal favor warning; research honors benches, techprints, and prerequisites; bill counts follow each recipe's limits; and name fields cap at the lengths the game really accepts.
  • Playing in a language other than English is far more reliable. Several features recognized things by matching English text on screen, including notification buttons, caravan destinations, stat breakdowns, scanner classification, and storage commands, and they broke quietly in translation. They now use the game's own internal names. Remaining hardcoded English was made translatable, names joined into lists follow each language's own word order, and spoken key names like Enter and Page Up translate too.
  • Cycling colonists with comma and period no longer freezes the game when a connected display has no signal, a common setup for players who do not need the picture. Unity reports a garbage screen size in that case, which sent the game's own colonist bar layout into a loop with no way out. It is guarded now, and colonist cycling keeps working with no display attached.
  • Fixed a crash to desktop during startup when an installed mod ships optional hooks into another mod that is not loaded, for example Progression: Core with VFE Tribals disabled. The tooltip scanner now skips anything it cannot safely inspect instead of taking the game down with it.
  • One broken mod can no longer take the reader down with it. A mod shipping an assembly that will not load on your platform used to silently disable command announcements for the whole game, and an error inside a screen's reader support left a silent window swallowing keystrokes. Both now contain themselves: the offending piece is skipped, or the screen says it failed and steps aside.
  • A family of focus bugs is gone, where a window opened from another screen came up buried underneath it, unreadable, with Escape closing the wrong thing. Naming a newborn from its birth letter, a confirmation from the Animals table, and an info card from the Factions tab were all affected. Windows opened from anywhere now speak and take input, and dialogs that pop up on their own, like the debug log after a mod error, no longer silence whatever is underneath.
  • Escape while editing a text field on one of the new game pages now only cancels the edit. Cancelling a colonist's name used to back out of the page underneath as well, and sometimes the page before that too. Enter behaves the same way: confirming a seed or a name finishes the edit without also advancing to the next page.
  • The xenotype editor and gene assembler got a round of repairs. Toggling a gene no longer collapses every category and throws the cursor to the top. Loading a xenotype now refreshes the selected-genes list and gene library immediately, and uses the same accessible file list as saving a game, with Delete removing a file after a confirmation. Collapse all and Expand all now move the categories the screen reader navigates too, and categories visibly open and close on screen. The unlabeled "..." button announces itself as "Name suggestions". Shift+Enter presses Save and apply, and Delete removes the focused gene. Save and apply now confirms the character was regenerated and reads their new details, matching the change a sighted player sees.
  • Columns that mods add to the Animals, Wildlife, and Mechs tables used to announce their cells as unavailable. They now read generically whenever the mod's column is built on a standard game column type, including each cell's tooltip. Enter also works on those cells now, so a dropdown column a mod adds opens its menu. The Traits column from Animal Traits System reads every animal's traits with their full descriptions, and the Spare Traits column says whether an animal is protected from auto-slaughter or marked for cull.
  • Empty screen sections no longer trap you outside them. Entering an empty list, such as the mods screen's disabled column when every mod is enabled, used to throw the cursor into another section and drop the empty one from the Tab cycle. Empty sections now stay reachable with Tab and announce themselves as empty.
  • Some mods add a search box to a dialog and hand it the keyboard the moment the dialog opens. That box then swallowed every arrow key and the dialog went completely silent; the bed assignment window from Sensible Bed Ownership was the first confirmed case. The mod now keeps the keyboard on every dialog it drives, whatever a mod focuses. Typing a name in that window jumps to the colonist, and Tab moves between the list and Close.
  • Acting on letters no longer discards them. Jumping to a letter's location or viewing its quest leaves refugee, visitor, birth, and other offer letters in the stack until you actually answer them, matching how the game itself treats each kind.
  • Forming a caravan from the world map no longer reads out the caravan dialog before it appears. The game hides that dialog while you pick a destination on the planet, so the mod now stays quiet about it until the route is confirmed and the dialog is really on screen.
  • In the precepts editor, setting or removing a precept keeps the cursor in the section you were working through and moves it to the next issue there, instead of following the issue into its new section. The announcement still says where the issue went, and the cursor only follows when the section you were in has emptied.
  • The pawn filter's reroll no longer strips what other mods give pawns at creation. The fast reroll loop rebuilt candidates without ever calling the full generator, so mods that hook it never ran: with Intimacy's Gender Works enabled, a health filter produced starting pawns the mod treats as sterile. When any mod hooks pawn generation, the reroll now regenerates each candidate through the same complete pipeline as the Randomize button. Searches run a little slower in heavily modded games.
  • Buttons that jump you to a thing's inspect tab now open the inspection tree with your cursor already on that tab's section. This covers vanilla's own jumps, like a death letter opening the combat log or a character card's social link, and mod buttons like Character Development's character rows; they used to open the tab visually and announce nothing. A button inside an inspect tab that opens a different main tab, such as Character Development's Add quirks, now opens that tab and hands it the keyboard, instead of bouncing back to the inspect pane or opening behind the tree. The tree keeps its place and returns when that tab closes.
  • Character Development's Characters tab is much improved. Enter on a character opens it for inspection with the cursor on their Wants section, instead of closing the tab and dropping you back on the map in silence. The tab now follows the mod's per-pawn reward points setting, so rewards no longer read as unavailable, each character's own points are spoken, and characters holding points with no wants are listed. Its Wants inspect tab reads properly too: the points bar is no longer three bare numbers, and every want and quirk is its own entry carrying its description and reward, with actions to reroll a want, dismiss it, add quirks, or remove one.
  • Progression: Education reads correctly now. Its Education tab reads the empty-class message, the classrooms description, and each classroom's color; the Knowledge panel reads a proficiency track even before a pawn has been granted a tier; and Enter no longer also creates or saves the class while you are assigning a teacher or student in its dialogs.
  • Form controls on a mod's own dialog now reach you complete. In the Additional controls section, a control with a very short label could be dropped, and a control drawn with its name beside it could arrive unnamed. Progression: Education's class dialog showed both, losing its subject picker and class hours outright and leaving its name, skill, and classroom fields unnamed. Nothing is dropped now unless we are certain it is already spoken elsewhere.
  • A slider whose ends are labelled with its own minimum and maximum now reads as a slider with a value, instead of reading those end labels as its name and setting. Progression: Education's semester goal slider announced "1,000 xp, slider, 100,000 xp" no matter where it was set, which made the target look like something that could not be changed.
  • A button that opens a mod's own window from one of our full-screen readers now hands that window the keyboard. Vanilla Factions Expanded - Tribals' Cornerstones button on the Factions screen was the clearest case: the window opened and read itself, but every key afterward still went to the faction list behind it. This is fixed for every screen at once, for any mod window that does not declare itself a modal dialog. The Tribals cornerstones window also announces your faction name and tells you the new ethos when unlocking a cornerstone rewrites it.
  • In the classic trade view, Enter on an item now opens the quantity chooser instead of arming the Accept confirmation. The Default Trade View and Default Work Menu View setting descriptions were rewritten for clarity, the classic view description no longer wrongly says Tab moves between the lists (it is Left and Right), and each view's description is read aloud when you open the picker to choose one.
  • Quieted spurious startup errors. The harmless missing-texture errors logged when playing without the Biotech DLC are gone, and errors on the storyteller selection page when another mod rewrites it are now warnings in the log rather than errors read aloud.
  • A batch of smaller fixes: opening a drug's settings in the drug policy manager reads each row as the checkbox, stepper, or slider it is instead of repeating the drug's name; drawing a straight line with the empty rectangle shape counts its cells once rather than twice; picking a new thing to build from a blueprint's gizmo menu right after placing something now places what you picked, not the previous building; the research tree moves a project into In progress once you start it instead of leaving it stuck under Available; saving your game returns you to the game rather than stranding you in the pause menu; and Page Up and Page Down on a starting character's skill land on that same skill for the next or previous character instead of jumping to the top of the list.
  • Dozens of other bugs were squashed, but this changelog is unreasonably long as it is. So why not play the game and find the new ones I left just for you? Yes, you, brave human, who managed to read through the entire changelog!

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.text: Common questions about what the mod does and doesn't do, and why.

docs.title: Can you add support for [some mod]?
docs.text:
Probably not, and almost certainly not any time soon. Here's the reasoning.

A lot of content mods, meaning mods that add new items, animals, events, or factions without building their own custom screens, are already largely accessible.

The trouble is mods that build their own UI. When a mod adds a custom screen that doesn't follow how vanilla RimWorld does things, the mod's screen gets no accessibility treatment from RimWorld Access. Making it accessible isn't a matter of flipping a switch. It means installing the mod, building a save that actually exercises that UI, writing and testing new Harmony patches for it, and then maintaining those patches whenever the mod updates. And that's for one mod.

Every time a new mod gets support, it opens the door to requests for the next one. The queue is effectively infinite. People in the Discord are finding new mods every week. I can't keep up with that, and trying to is how burnout happens.

There's also a localization problem most people don't think about. Many mods haven't been translated into the languages RimWorld Access supports. When a mod's text isn't localized, players hear the raw English strings, and the question comes back to me rather than to the mod author. That's not something I'm willing to volunteer for.

The codebase also isn't in a state right now where I can safely take outside pull requests for mod accessibility. That may change. Even if it does, though, I have no interest in becoming a code reviewer for mods I may not even have installed. Reviewing a contribution properly would mean installing whoever's mods to test the change, and I'm not going to approve work I can't check. So even down the road, this may simply not be something I take on. We'll see.

None of this is permanent. Once the core RimWorld experience is solid, I'll probably give some mods attention. The Vanilla Expanded series is a likely candidate, because those authors do careful work and their content fits naturally with what the mod does. I may also cover mods I personally find interesting. Eventually, once I'm more comfortable taking this on, I might set up community polls so players can weigh in on which mods matter most to them to see made accessible. I'd like people to have a say in what I work on, if I ever get there.

But the baseline answer is: if a mod adds its own custom screens, don't expect support for it.

docs.title: Why doesn't Alt+H read out every health condition?
docs.text:
Alt+H is a quick readout for what matters in a hurry: consciousness, movement, manipulation, and bleeding status. Those four things tell you most of what you need to know when something urgent is happening.

The request that comes up most often is adding infection status to that readout. The trouble is length. If a pawn has several infections or conditions, hearing them all in one announcement is slower than just searching for the one you care about. And searching is something the mod is already good at.

Type-ahead is, more or less, a search filter, and it's basically a mouse for blind people. Once it clicks, you'll use it everywhere. Here's how it works for health. Press Enter on the pawn under your cursor, or Ctrl+Alt+Enter on a pawn you've selected from the colonist bar, to open that pawn's inspect screen. Then just start typing. Type "inf" and you land on infections. Type "leg", "arm", or "head", or even just "hea", and you land on everything wrong with that part. The arrow keys step through the other matches. It's faster than any fixed readout could be, because you go straight to what you asked for.

That said, I'm still thinking about how best to surface every status condition through another shortcut, probably Alt+Shift+H. I'm not against the idea. It just feels redundant when type-ahead already gets you there so quickly. If you've leaned on type-ahead and still feel something is missing, that's worth telling me.

docs.title: Is there a guide to laying out a base?
docs.text:
Not in this documentation, and that's deliberate. Base layout is genuinely hard to describe in text. A kill box or a storage warehouse has a visual logic that's difficult to convey through written coordinates and dimensions, and advice that sounds simple on paper ("make your bedrooms seven by seven on the exterior, five by five inside") can be tricky to apply in practice.

What this documentation covers is the mechanics: how to place buildings, how rooms work, what the Architect menu offers, how to use the scanner to survey your map. The strategy of what to build and where is a harder problem.

The colony building guide on the RimWorld wiki is a good place to start. It's written for players generally, and the advice translates.

For the "how does this actually look in practice" question, the goal is eventually to collect save files from community members that demonstrate well-built bases, so you can load them up and explore. That's not ready yet. The best current resource is the RimWorld Access Discord, where players share their approaches and can answer specific layout questions.

docs.title: Can I play with other mods?
docs.text:
You can, but it's unsupported. When something breaks in a modded game, it's very hard to tell whether the issue is with RimWorld Access, with one of the other mods, or with a combination. Isolating a bug officially means testing with only Harmony and RimWorld Access active, and if you're playing a modded save, that's not easy to do without starting over.

This doesn't mean you should avoid mods. Plenty of players run large mod lists without problems. But if you run into a bug and want to report it, you'll likely need to be able to reproduce it in a clean environment before it can be investigated. See reporting bugs for what that looks like.

The mod doesn't police what you install. It just can't take responsibility for what other mods do.

docs.title: Should I use permadeath (commitment mode)?
docs.text:
You can, but go in knowing the risks. In commitment mode, if your colony ends, the save is gone. Software crashes, screen reader hiccups, and bugs in any of your mods can all end a run without warning. The mod is stable enough that many players use commitment mode without incident, but "stable enough" and "completely safe" aren't the same thing.

If you're new to RimWorld, the bigger risk is just the game's difficulty. Losing a long permadeath run to a game mechanic you didn't know about yet is frustrating in a way that reloading from a normal save isn't. Most experienced players recommend playing without commitment mode until you understand how to handle raids, disease, and starvation.

If you want to use it, go for it. Just keep in mind that no software is crash-proof, and that mod updates, game updates, and screen reader updates can all introduce unexpected behavior.

docs.title: Some text isn't in my language. Why?
docs.text:
RimWorld Access supports several languages, and text that comes from the mod itself (menu labels, navigation announcements, and the descriptions I write) should appear in your language where it has been translated. Localization is still fairly new, though, so some of the mod's own text may not be translated yet, and there are still genuine localization bugs to work out. If you hear English where you expect your own language in a base-game or RimWorld Access screen, please report it. See reporting bugs. That kind of report genuinely helps.

Some text can also come from another mod you have installed. Mods are responsible for their own translations, and when a mod author hasn't provided one for your language, that text falls back to English. That part isn't mine to fix, since the translation isn't mine to provide for content I didn't write. It isn't always obvious which mod a piece of text comes from, which is why these questions often land here, but the place to ask for a mod's translation is with that mod's author.

docs.title: Keyboard reference
docs.text: Every key the mod uses, grouped by where you use it. The same key can do different things depending on the screen you're on, so this page is organized by context. One short note on context-sensitivity appears at the end.

docs.title: Global
docs.text:
These work most of the time while a game is running.

Key What it does Tab Open the Architect menu (build) F1 Work tab F2 Schedule tab F3 Assign tab F4 Animals tab, or Mechs, or a chooser if you have both F5 Wildlife tab F6 Research tab F7 Quests tab F8 Toggle the world map on or back off F9 History tab F12 Extra menus picker: Factions, plus Ideology if that DLC is active Space Pause and unpause Shift+1 Normal game speed Shift+2 Fast game speed Shift+3 Superfast game speed T Announce the current time, date, weather, and season Alt+T Announce current game speed, whether the game is paused, and performance (ticks per second) ? Open the Learning Helper (RimWorld's built-in tutorial tips) Z Search by name (on the map, feeds the scanner) Escape Cancel, close, or back out

docs.title: On the map
docs.text: These act on the tile under the cursor, or on the selected pawn.

docs.title: Moving around
docs.text:
Key What it does Arrow keys Move the cursor one tile; the camera follows Ctrl+Arrow Jump using the current jump mode Shift+Up / Shift+Down Cycle the jump mode forward or backward (the cursor does not move) Shift+Left / Shift+Right Adjust the preset jump distance by 1 (Preset Distance mode only) Shift+Ctrl+Left / Shift+Ctrl+Right Adjust the preset jump distance by 10 Ctrl+G Open the coordinate jump dialog. Type X, then press comma or Space, then type Z. Blank field keeps the current coordinate. Prefix with + or - for a relative offset

Four jump modes are available: Preset Distance (the default), Impassable, Terrain, and Structure. Cycle between them with Shift+Up / Shift+Down. See the map page for what each one lands on.

docs.title: Tile info (number keys)
docs.text:
The mod announces much of this automatically as you arrow around. These keys are on-demand spot checks for the detail you want.

Key What it reads 1 Items and pawns at the cursor 2 Terrain (label, fertility, smoothness, beauty, cleanliness, path cost) 3 Harvestable things: plants (species, growth, harvestable or dying); with the right DLC and equipment, also fish and deep-scanner mineral targets 4 Light, brightness, and temperature 5 Room stats 6 Power 7 Areas this tile belongs to

On the world map the number keys mean different things. See World and caravans.

docs.title: Selecting pawns
docs.text:
For the full walkthrough, see Selecting pawns.

Key What it does Comma / Period Cycle to the previous or next colonist Alt+1 ... Alt+0 Select colonist 1 through 10 Alt+Down Page to colonists 11-20 (then Alt+1-0 to select within that page) Alt+Left / Alt+Right Move through pawns on the colonist bar Ctrl+Alt+Left / Ctrl+Alt+Right Reorder the selected pawn along the colonist bar Alt+Space Multi-select (mainly for combat; multi-select breaks many gizmos that expect a single pawn) Ctrl+Shift+F1-F4 Save the current selection as a combat group Ctrl+F1-F4 Recall a saved combat group / Focus the cursor pawn on the colonist or mech bar Alt+C Jump the cursor to the selected pawn and keep it riding along (or open a chooser if several are selected)

docs.title: Pawns at a glance
docs.text:
These prioritize whatever is under the cursor, then fall back to the pawn selected with comma/period or Alt+number.

Key What it reads Alt+H Health Alt+M Mood Alt+N Needs Alt+G Gear Alt+K Top 3 skills Alt+P Skills table for all colonists Alt+B Read the selected pawn's combat log (10 most recent battle entries)

Alt+H, Alt+M, Alt+N, and Alt+G work on your pawns, enemy pawns, and animals. Alt+P opens a sortable table covering every colonist.

For checking on pawns in depth, see Checking on pawns.

docs.title: Acting on the map
docs.text: Key What it does Alt+F Un-forbid every item on the map at once Alt+A Assign an allowed area to the selected pawn (prioritizes the cursor) Alt+I Open the info card for whatever the cursor is on, or for the item referenced in a menu G Open the gizmo menu for the object under the cursor ] Open the context menu for the tile under the cursor [ Carry out the top context-menu option immediately Shift+[ Queue the top option instead of replacing the current one

docs.title: Drafting and giving orders
docs.text:
How you control pawns in a fight. The combat page covers these in depth.

Key What it does R Draft or undraft the selected pawn

docs.title: Targeting a weapon or ability
docs.text:
After starting an attack from the gizmo menu (G, choose the attack, then Enter):

Key What it does Arrow keys, then Enter Move the cursor to the target, Enter to fire Escape Cancel targeting R Announce distance, whether the target is in range, and line of sight T Announce who is caught in an area-of-effect ability at the cursor

Targeting stays open if the target is invalid or out of range, and tells you why, so you can adjust and retry.

docs.title: Opening detail screens
docs.text: Key What it does Enter Inspect the thing under the cursor Ctrl+Alt+Enter Open the inspect view for the selected pawn (the one chosen on the colonist bar)

docs.title: The scanner
docs.text:
The scanner steps through categories, subcategories, item types, and individual instances, then lets you jump straight to a target.

Key What it does Ctrl+Page Up / Ctrl+Page Down Move between categories Shift+Page Up / Shift+Page Down Move between subcategories Page Up / Page Down Move between item types (ordered by distance) Alt+Page Up / Alt+Page Down Move between individual instances within a group Home Jump the cursor to the nearest tile in the current target. Press again while standing on the target to jump to its center End Announce distance and direction to the scanner target Alt+Home Toggle scanner auto-jump mode (the scanner jumps the cursor automatically when you change categories)

Home also pairs with the search: run a Z search, press Enter to focus the scanner on the result, then Home to jump to it.

docs.title: Building placement
docs.text:
Once you have picked a designator in the Architect menu, place it on the map with these.

Key What it does Space Set a point (first corner, then second) Shift+Space Remove the last placed point or blueprint at the cursor Enter Confirm and place the designation = (or +) Add another shape, keeping the blueprints already placed - Remove the last placed segment Ctrl+A Select all: steps from the enclosing area, to the whole map, to nothing Ctrl+Shift+A Step back one level of select-all scope Tab Switch the designator's shape (filled rectangle, empty rectangle, manual)

The jump-mode keys from Moving around (Ctrl+Arrow to jump, Shift+Left/Right to adjust the distance) are how you extend a shape to an exact size before setting the second point.

docs.title: Menus and tables
docs.text:
These apply across the mod's menus, tree views, and tables.

Key What it does Tab / Shift+Tab Move between the panels of a screen Up / Down Move between items or rows Left / Right Move between columns or categories; in a tree, collapse or expand Home / End Jump to the first or last item Type any text Type-ahead: jump to the matching entry. Works in every menu and list Enter / Space Select, deselect, or toggle a checkbox Alt+S In a table: sort by the selected column. In a dialog or filter: save, confirm, or advance Shift+8 (asterisk) Expand all sibling nodes at the current tree level

docs.title: The Enter versus Alt+S rule
docs.text: In a screen where Enter selects and deselects items, Alt+S is what confirms the screen and moves forward. If Enter does nothing special on that screen, Enter finishes it. See Navigating menus for the full story.

docs.title: In tables specifically
docs.text:
Tables typically show pawns as rows and attributes as columns. On top of the keys above:

Key What it does Alt+S Sort by the selected column; press again to toggle descending, ascending, then clear Shift+Up / Shift+Down Paint the current cell's value onto the rows above or below Shift+Home / Shift+End Paint from the current row to the top or bottom Ctrl+Shift+Home / Ctrl+Shift+End Paint the column across every row = / - Adjust a numeric cell by one (Enter to type a number) ] Open a context menu for that column, category, or cell

docs.title: World and caravans
docs.text: On the world map (F8), several keys take on travel-specific meanings.

docs.title: Tile info (number keys, world map)
docs.text:
Key What it reads 1 Growing conditions: growing period, rainfall, forageability, grazing, stone types 2 Movement and travel cost: difficulty, terrain, hilliness, elevation, roads, rivers 3 Disease frequency (and pollution or haze fields with the right DLC) 4 Time zone and global coordinates 5 Regions and landmarks

Biome is announced when you arrow onto a tile, not via a number key.

docs.title: Travel and caravans
docs.text:
Key What it does C Start choosing a caravan route (add one or more waypoints) R Open the route planner to preview paths and travel times Space Set a waypoint (or re-announce the current tile during site selection) Enter Inspect a caravan or enter your own settlement at the cursor. During site selection, confirm settling there Comma / Period Cycle between your caravans Ctrl+Space Add or remove a caravan from a multi-selection (then merge them with the caravan's G gizmo) Alt+A Toggle auto-provision (lets the game pick supplies) Alt+S Send the caravan ] Act on the tile: travel to, trade with, attack, settle, and so on G Open the selected caravan's gizmos: settle, split, rest, merge Delete Remove a pawn or item from the caravan F8 Toggle the world view off and return to the colony Alt+Home Jump to your colony Alt+J Toggle world-map scanner auto-jump mode End Announce distance and direction to the world scanner target Alt+End Jump to the nearest caravan

Enter does not settle a tile from the in-game world map. Settling is done via a gizmo on the caravan. See Caravans and The world map.

docs.title: Trade window
docs.text:
When trading with a visiting trader, a settlement, or an orbital trader, the trade screen uses these. The classic view (the default) is three sections you Tab between; the table view is one sortable list with a column cursor.

Key What it does Up / Down Move through the goods, or adjust the quantity by 1 in the quantity chooser Left / Right Switch sections in the classic view (the trader's items, the trade summary, your items); move between columns in the table view; walk the toolbar Tab / Shift+Tab Hop between the goods and the toolbar, returning to the section and row you left + / - Adjust the quantity by 1 Shift+Up / Shift+Down Adjust the quantity by 10 Ctrl+Up / Ctrl+Down Adjust the quantity by 100 Shift+Home / Shift+End Max sell or max buy; plain Home / End do the same inside the quantity chooser Home / End Jump to the first or last item Enter Open or leave the quantity chooser for the current item; on the balance line, read both sides' silver Type a number In the quantity chooser, set a quantity (lead with - to sell, + to buy) Ctrl+Tab Switch between the classic and table views Alt+A Accept the trade Alt+B Announce the silver (or favor) on each side Alt+P Price breakdown for the current item Alt+I Info card for the current item Alt+L Open the trader's sellable-items list Alt+G Toggle gift mode (give goods for goodwill) Delete or Alt+R Reset the current item; Shift+Alt+R resets everything Escape Close the trade

docs.title: Context-dependent keys
docs.text:
A handful of keys do different jobs depending on where you are. This is normal behavior shared by most applications; the list below is for reference when a key does something unexpected.

  • R: on the colony map, draft or undraft; on the world map, jump to a random tile (site selection) or open the route planner; during targeting, announce distance and range.
  • Alt+F: on the colony map, un-forbid every item; during pawn creation, open the reroll filters.
  • Alt+A: on the colony map, assign an allowed area; in caravan formation, toggle auto-provision; in the Quests tab, accept the quest; in a trade, accept the trade.
  • Alt+M: on the colony map, read a pawn's mood; in the Work tab, toggle between manual and basic priority mode.
  • Alt+B: on the colony map, read a pawn's combat log; in a trade, announce the silver/favor balance.
  • Alt+G: on the colony map, read a pawn's gear; in a trade, toggle gift mode.
  • Alt+P: on the colony map, open the skills table; in a trade, show the price breakdown.
  • Alt+R: during pawn creation, reroll the current pawn; in a trade, reset the current item.
  • Alt+S: in a table, sort by the selected column; in a dialog or filter, save or advance; in caravan formation, send the caravan.

Mac users: see Playing on Mac for how modifier keys map on macOS.

docs.title: Where to learn RimWorld
docs.text: These docs teach you the mod: which keys do what, how the screens work, how to drive RimWorld from the keyboard. They are not a strategy guide. RimWorld is a deep game, and the learning resources that exist for it are extensive. This page points to the ones I recommend.

docs.title: My tutorial video
docs.text:
I recorded a walkthrough of my first accessible game. It covers the early colony arc from landing through first threats, narrated as I go.

Watch the RimWorld Access tutorial

docs.title: The RimWorld wiki
docs.text:
rimworldwiki.com is the authoritative reference for game mechanics. It covers everything: temperature and food spoilage, what each trait does, the mood system, the health system, how raids scale. It is large and actively maintained. RimWorld Access mirrors vanilla RimWorld closely, so the learning resources written for the wider community work for you too.

The wiki's own Basics overview is a good first read if you want an overview of the game's flow before diving in. A few articles I find myself returning to:

  • Work: how work priorities and job types interact
  • Recruitment and Resistance: getting prisoners and downed enemies to join
  • Trade price improvement: what actually moves prices
  • Comms console: calling traders and contacting other factions
  • Allowed areas: restricting where colonists can go
  • Ideology: the belief-system and ritual mechanics (DLC)
  • Health and Medicine: how treatment, injuries, and diseases work

docs.title: RimWorld YouTubers
docs.text:
For strategy and a feel for how experienced players think, RimWorld has a large community of creators on YouTube. Narrated playthroughs work well by ear: the player talks through priorities, explains decisions, and signals when to worry and when to relax. Putting a beginner playthrough on in the background is one of the faster ways to absorb the game's rhythms.

I learned the game from sighted players and YouTubers before this mod existed, and that approach still holds up.

docs.title: Prior art in blind gaming
docs.text:
Before RimWorld Access, blind players had very few games of this depth to play. If you are coming from the blind gaming community, the closest familiar reference is Castaways by Aprone, a survival and colony game that has long been a well-regarded option for blind players. Castaways is available here.

Other complex management games, like Oxygen Not Included, became accessible after RimWorld Access. If you have played one of them, the genre's logic will carry over.

docs.title: Start gentle
docs.text:
The single best piece of advice for a new player: start on a low difficulty or peaceful.

RimWorld's difficulty range is enormous. On peaceful, raids are infrequent and mild, and there is breathing room to learn the controls and the rhythms of colony life without a crisis every few minutes. Once the keyboard feels natural and you have run a colony for a while, a harder start will make a lot more sense. There is no reason to learn the controls and survive a death spiral at the same time. You do not need to start a new game to raise the difficulty later: you can adjust it in settings on a running save.

Your first colony is supposed to be a bit of a mess. That is how it goes for everyone.

docs.title: Playing on Mac
docs.text: This page covers the keyboard differences between Windows and macOS. All other documentation uses Windows key names. Substitute as described here when reading any other page.

docs.title: General modifier substitutions
docs.text:
Windows macOS Ctrl Cmd Alt Option

These substitutions apply throughout the mod. For example, where the docs say Ctrl+Alt+Enter, on Mac you press Cmd+Option+Enter.

docs.title: The Ctrl+Tab exception
docs.text:
One shortcut does not follow the Ctrl-to-Cmd pattern: Ctrl+Tab (used to switch views in the Work menu and similar panels) maps to Option+Tab on macOS, not Cmd+Tab.

This is because Cmd+Tab is reserved by the operating system as the app switcher and cannot reach the game, and physical Ctrl+Tab is also not reliably deliverable on Mac through Unity. The mod handles this automatically: when the current key is Tab, pressing Option acts as the Ctrl substitute. No configuration is needed.

So on Mac:

Windows macOS Ctrl+Tab Option+Tab Ctrl+Shift+Tab Option+Shift+Tab

All other Ctrl shortcuts use Cmd as normal.

docs.title: Reporting bugs
docs.text: Found something broken? A clear report gets it fixed faster, and it does not take much.

docs.title: First, isolate it
docs.text:
Test with only Harmony and RimWorld Access enabled, and no other mods. Other mods can change how the game behaves in ways that look like a RimWorld Access bug but aren't. If the problem still happens with just those two mods, it's a real report.

This is genuinely hard once you have other mods installed: stripping them out can break the save you were playing, so reproducing a problem in a clean setup takes real effort. RimWorld Access officially supports only Harmony plus itself, so a report from a clean save is the most useful kind, but do what you can.

docs.title: What to include
docs.text:
A good report answers three questions:

  • What you did. The screen you were on and the keys you pressed, step by step. "On the Work tab, I pressed Alt+M, then..." is the right level of detail.
  • What was announced. What your screen reader actually said.
  • What you expected instead.

If you can, include your screen reader, your operating system, and which DLC was active. The more reliably you can reproduce it, the easier it is to fix.

docs.title: Attach your log file
docs.text:
RimWorld writes a log every time it runs, called Player.log. It records errors that never appear on screen, so attaching it often points straight at the cause. The file is replaced each time the game launches, so grab it after the problem happens and before starting the game again.

It is located here:

  • Windows: %localappdata%low\Ludeon Studios\RimWorld by Ludeon Studios\Player.log
  • macOS: ~/Library/Logs/Ludeon Studios/RimWorld by Ludeon Studios/Player.log

You can paste either path as-is to reach the file. On Windows, paste it into the Run dialog (Win+R) or the File Explorer address bar. On macOS, paste it into Finder's Go to Folder box (Cmd+Shift+G).

docs.title: Where to file it
docs.text:
The easiest place is the #bug-reports channel on the RimWorld Access Discord server.

If you know your way around GitHub, you can also open a GitHub issue instead.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: RimWorld Access has its own options panel, separate from RimWorld's standard mod settings. Reach it from the main menu under Options, then RimWorld Access. The panel is available both at the main menu and in-game, so changes take effect immediately.

docs.title: Wrap navigation
docs.text:
Default: off.

When on, menus loop from the last item back to the first, and from the first back to the last. When off, navigation stops at the boundaries and plays a short tone to tell you the cursor could not move, rather than reading the same row to you again.

docs.title: Announce position
docs.text:
Default: on.

When on, announcements include a position indicator such as "3 of 7." Turn this off if the count feels like noise.

docs.title: Show pawn activity on map cursor movement
docs.text:
Default: on.

When on, arrowing over a non-colonist pawn (an animal, visitor, raider, or other non-colonist) announces what activity that pawn is performing. This information is inferred from the pawn's current state. If it feels like an unfair advantage, keep it off.

docs.title: Show cover info for drafted and hostile pawns
docs.text:
Default: on.

When on, cover information is included in the cursor announcement for drafted pawns and hostile pawns. For example: "Bob, behind sandbag (good cover), melee attacking." Applies during combat.

docs.title: Announce terrain on cursor movement
docs.text:
Default: on.

When on, the terrain name is spoken each time the cursor moves to a new tile. The terrain sound effect plays independently of this setting.

docs.title: Announce depth levels in treeviews
docs.text:
Default: on.

When on, moving deeper into a tree view announces the level number, for example "level 2." Turn this off if you navigate tree views fluently and find the level announcements redundant.

docs.title: Rashad Hates Treeviews (submenu-style navigation)
docs.text:
Default: off.

This is a toggle that changes how tree views behave across the mod. Named after another accessibility-mod developer, Rashad, who is not a fan of the traditional tree-view interaction pattern. (His own mods use tree views all over the place, just under other names, but the name stuck.)

Off (standard tree view):

  • Right arrow on a collapsed item expands it, revealing its children alongside the parent.
  • Right arrow on an already-expanded item moves into its first child.
  • The parent stays visible in the list alongside its children.

On (submenu mode):

  • Right arrow on an item expands it, hides the parent, and places you directly on the first child. It feels like stepping into a submenu.
  • Left arrow collapses back to the parent.
  • Your last position inside each parent is remembered when you return.

There is no wrong choice here, just preferences. Submenu mode keeps lists short and moves you forward quickly. Standard mode keeps parents and children visible together, which can help with orientation in a large tree. Try both.

For how tree views work in general, see Navigating menus.

docs.title: Default Work Menu View (F1)
docs.text:
Default: Focused.

Determines which view opens when you press F1.

  • Focused: a priority-grouped per-pawn view. Lower verbosity; well suited for checking on individual colonists.
  • Table: pawn rows by work-type columns, mirroring vanilla. Supports sorting and painting.

You can switch between views at any time from within the Work menu using Ctrl+Tab (or Option+Tab on macOS). The setting updates automatically to remember your last choice.

docs.title: Announce forced slowdowns from threats
docs.text:
Default: off.

When on, the mod announces when the game forces Normal speed because of a nearby threat ("Game slowed down by presence of threat") and again when the slowdown lifts. This only fires if your chosen speed is faster than Normal.

To check the current game speed at any time, press Alt+T.

docs.title: Announce selected pawn activity
docs.text:
Default: off.

When on, the mod narrates what the selected pawn is doing, for as long as they stay selected: each new job as it starts ("Cutting plants", "Hauling steel to stockpile"), and each named room or zone they walk into ("in kitchen", "in growing zone 1"). Outdoors, and in rooms the game gives no role to, nothing is spoken.

Moving the map cursor ends the narration. Select the pawn again with comma, period, or the colonist bar to pick it back up, or press Alt+C to send the cursor to them, which keeps the narration going while the cursor rides along. See Selecting pawns.

Setting tooltips are expanding as localization work continues. If a setting's in-game tooltip is not yet in your language, the English tooltip is still shown.

docs.title: Creating your colonists
docs.text:
This is the last screen before the game starts: the character setup screen, where you decide who lands with you. You can read each candidate's background, reroll ones you dislike, set filters to control what the game generates, and rename anyone. The colonists you keep here are the ones you will be keeping alive for the rest of the game.

The screen is a tree view (see Navigating menus). Use Up and Down to move through the list of candidates, Right to expand one and read its details, and Left to collapse it again.

docs.title: The slots: Selected and Left Behind
docs.text:
The screen shows up to eight candidate slots even if your scenario only starts you with three colonists. The list is divided by two markers: Selected and Left Behind. Pawns in the Selected group come with you when the game starts. Pawns in the Left Behind group do not. As you arrow across the boundary, the mod announces which group you have entered.

The extra slots exist for rerolling. You can reroll a Left Behind slot as many times as you like looking for a good candidate, then move that pawn up into the Selected group.

docs.title: Moving a pawn between groups
docs.text: Press Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down to move the current candidate up or down the list. When a pawn crosses the Selected/Left Behind boundary, the mod announces which group they landed in and who their new neighbors are.

docs.title: Reading a pawn's details
docs.text:
Press Right on a candidate to expand them. Inside you find categories you can expand in turn:

  • Bio: their backstory and background.
  • Age: RimWorld tracks two ages. Biological age is how old the body is; chronological age is how many years have passed since birth. The two can differ due to cryptosleep stasis.
  • Relations: other pawns this candidate knows, with opinions in each relation's detail. Press Enter on a relation to jump to that pawn in the list.
  • Traits: personality traits. Most pawns have at least one, up to three.
  • Incapable of: work types this pawn refuses to do. Worth checking before you commit to keeping someone.
  • Skills: their twelve skill levels (0 to 20) and passions. A passion makes a pawn learn a skill faster and gain a mood boost from doing it. Skills come with no passion, a single passion, or a double (burning) passion.
  • Health and possessions round out the picture.

When a category is collapsed, the mod reads a short summary so you can decide whether to expand. The collapsed pawn entry itself carries age, gender, traits, and top skills inline.

docs.title: Comparing the same detail across pawns
docs.text: Once you have expanded to a particular detail on one pawn, Page Up and Page Down jump to the same spot on the previous or next pawn. If you are on the Construction skill for candidate one, Page Down takes you to Construction on candidate two, and so on. This makes it easy to compare one attribute across everyone without re-navigating each pawn's tree.

docs.title: Rerolling and filtering
docs.text:
If you do not like a candidate, you can generate a new one. Filters let you tell the game what to look for before it generates.

Pressing ] on a candidate opens a context menu gathering these actions in one place: randomize (the same as Alt+R), rename (the same as Alt+N), and edit the pawn filter (the same as Alt+F). With the Biotech DLC it also includes the developmental stage and xenotype options described below. Each has a direct key as well, so you can use whichever you prefer.

docs.title: Reroll (Alt+R)
docs.text: Press Alt+R to reroll the candidate you are on. A new pawn replaces them. If you have filters active, the game rerolls behind the scenes until it finds someone who matches (or hits the roll limit), then tells you how many attempts it took.

docs.title: Filters (Alt+F)
docs.text:
Press Alt+F to open the pawn filter editor. Filters constrain what reroll will accept. You might ask for a colonist with Shooting 8 and no Pyromaniac trait, then reroll until you get one. This is not a native RimWorld feature: it is a rebuild of Random Plus, a mod popular with sighted players. New players can ignore it and just reroll by hand; it is here for when you want finer control. Filters persist across new games.

The editor is a flat list grouped into sections. Use Up and Down to move through it.

  • Minimum skill levels: for each of the twelve skills, use Left and Right to set a minimum level, or Shift+Left and Shift+Right to jump in larger steps. Press Enter on a skill row to cycle the required passion (none, then single, then double). Shift+Home and Shift+End snap a value to its minimum or maximum.
  • Passion counts: set a minimum and maximum number of total passions across all skills, adjusted with Left and Right.
  • Age: minimum and maximum, adjusted with Left and Right.
  • Required traits and excluded traits: navigate to the "add required trait" or "add excluded trait" row, then press Enter to open a trait picker. Type to search (typing "pyr" finds Pyromaniac, a trait you do not want), then press Enter to select. To remove a trait you have added, navigate to it and press Delete.
  • Roll limit: the maximum number of reroll attempts before the game gives up and keeps the last result.

Press Alt+S to save your filters and close the editor. Escape also closes the editor.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: Near the bottom of the filter list are preset options. You can save the current filter set as a named preset and load a saved one later. Because presets persist across games, you can build a "balanced starter" filter once and reuse it for every new colony.

docs.title: The Team Skills summary (Tab)
docs.text: Press Tab to switch to the Team Skills summary, which covers everyone currently in the Selected group. It lists the skills the game treats as important for a starting colony, which is most but not all of the twelve. For each listed skill it tells you the best pawn at that skill, their level, and their passion. Press Up and Down to move through the skills, or type to jump to one by name. Press Tab again to return to the candidate list.

docs.title: Renaming a pawn (Alt+N)
docs.text: Press Alt+N to rename the candidate you are on. You can set their first name, nickname, and last name. The nickname is what the game usually uses, so a clear, distinct nickname makes everyone easier to track. This is your chance to set a pawn's first and last name: you cannot change those once the game starts. With the Biotech DLC there is a brief 24-hour window to name a newborn child, but otherwise names are fixed at the start.

docs.title: Starting the game
docs.text: When you are happy with your roster, press Enter to confirm. The game asks you to confirm starting with the colonists you have chosen. Confirm, and the game begins.

docs.title: Picking a xenotype (Biotech DLC)
docs.text: With the Biotech DLC, each candidate has a xenotype representing their genetic makeup, with most baseline humans set to Baseliner. To change it, press ] on a pawn to open its context menu and choose the xenotype option. That opens a list of every xenotype in the game, plus an option to create a custom one in a gene editor. Picking a xenotype rerolls the pawn as that type. Developmental stage (baby, child, adult) is also on this menu. For how the context menu works, see The context menu.

docs.title: Starting a new game
docs.text:
Selecting New Colony from the main menu opens a short setup flow: choose a scenario, then a storyteller, difficulty, and save mode, then configure the world. This page covers those screens in order. The next two pages cover choosing a landing site and creating your colonists.

Each screen advances with Enter when you are done, and Escape goes back to the previous screen.

docs.title: Choosing a scenario
docs.text:
A scenario sets the starting rules: who your colonists are, what equipment they begin with, and what conditions apply throughout the game. When the screen opens, the mod announces the current scenario's name, summary, and category.

Use Up and Down to move through the scenario list. The mod announces the name, summary, and category of each scenario as you navigate. Type letters to jump to a scenario by name (typeahead search).

The default, Crashlanded, starts you with three survivors and some basic supplies. The Rich Explorer starts with one well-equipped colonist; Lost Tribe starts with more people and less technology. The choice has a meaningful effect on the early game.

docs.title: Reading the scenario details
docs.text: Press Tab to switch to the detail panel for the selected scenario. The detail panel is a tree view listing the starting colonists, starting items, items scattered on the map, and any special conditions. Use Up and Down to move through the entries, Right to expand a node, and Left to collapse it. Press Tab or Escape to return to the scenario list.

docs.title: Editing or copying a scenario
docs.text:
Press Alt+E to open the selected scenario in the editor. If the scenario is a built-in or another user's Workshop upload, the mod creates an editable copy for you and says so. If it is your own custom or Workshop scenario, it opens directly for editing.

The scenario editor is a separate page with its own navigation. When you are done in the editor, the screen returns you to the scenario list.

docs.title: Selecting a scenario
docs.text: Press Enter on the scenario list to confirm the highlighted scenario and advance to the next screen. If the Scenario Builder entry is selected, Enter opens the Scenario Builder instead.

docs.title: Choosing a storyteller, difficulty, and save mode
docs.text:
This screen contains three sections cycled with Tab and Shift+Tab: storyteller, difficulty, and save mode. The mod announces which section you are in when you switch.

Within each section, press Up and Down to move between options, and type to search by name.

docs.title: Storyteller
docs.text:
The storyteller controls the pacing and style of events that hit your colony.

  • Cassandra Classic sends a steadily escalating challenge. This is the default and the most common choice.
  • Phoebe Chillax spaces events out and gives more breathing room. A calmer pace if you want to build without constant pressure.
  • Randy Random does whatever it wants. Sometimes quiet, sometimes three raids in a row.

For the differences in how each storyteller behaves, see the Storyteller article on the RimWorld wiki.

docs.title: Difficulty
docs.text:
Press Tab to move to the difficulty section, then Up and Down to choose. Each option reads its name and a short description.

There is also a Custom difficulty option. Press Enter on Custom to open the custom difficulty editor, which exposes individual sliders for threat scale, population cap, disease frequency, trade prices, and many other factors. You can adjust these sliders at any time during a running save, so there is no pressure to get them exactly right before you start.

For a description of what each preset difficulty changes, see the Difficulty article on the RimWorld wiki.

docs.title: Save mode
docs.text:
Press Tab to move to the save mode section, then Up and Down to choose:

  • Reload anytime lets you save and load freely.
  • Commitment mode keeps a single rolling save you cannot reload. Events are permanent.

When all three sections are set, press Enter to advance to the world configuration screen.

docs.title: Anomaly settings (Anomaly DLC)
docs.text: If the Anomaly DLC is active, a fourth section appears after save mode. Press Tab to reach it. The Anomaly Settings dialog is already open at that point, so there is nothing to confirm to open it: you are placed directly in the dialog, which lets you set the anomaly playstyle and adjust related sliders. Press Alt+S to accept your changes, or Escape to discard them and return to the storyteller screen.

docs.title: World configuration
docs.text:
This screen lets you set the world seed and adjust parameters such as planet coverage, rainfall, and temperature. It is a list of sliders; press Up and Down to move between them and Left and Right to adjust the current one. Press Enter on the Seed field to type a seed directly.

The defaults produce a valid world, and the seed is randomized automatically. This screen is mainly useful for experienced players who want a specific type of world.

Press Enter to generate the world. After generation, the world map opens for you to choose a landing site.

For information about how world generation parameters affect the planet, see the World generation article on the RimWorld wiki.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Choosing a landing site on the world map.
  • Creating your colonists, the screen after you settle.

docs.title: Choosing a landing site
docs.text: After the world generates, the world map opens so you can pick where your colony will be. Your job here is to find a tile you like and settle it. The navigation you learn here carries over to the same map you will use later for caravans and travel.

docs.title: Moving around the map
docs.text:
Arrow keys move the cursor one tile at a time and the camera follows. When you move onto a tile, the mod announces the biome name and a short summary of conditions. Use this to get a quick read on the terrain as you explore.

A few shortcuts make navigation faster:

  • R jumps the cursor to a random valid starting tile and reads its details. A generated world holds tens of thousands of tiles, so this lands you somewhere new each time you press it.
  • Space re-announces the current tile.
  • Ctrl+Up/Down/Left/Right jumps to the next biome boundary in that direction, useful for finding the edge of a desert or the start of a forest.

docs.title: Reading tile details
docs.text:
When the cursor is on a tile, the number keys 1 through 5 each read a specific category of information. These are on-demand spot checks; much of this information is already announced as you arrow around, so you do not need to press these after every move.

  • 1 reads growing conditions: the growing period, rainfall, forageability percentage and food type, whether animals can graze, and stone types available for mining.
  • 2 reads movement and travel cost: movement difficulty (including any road multiplier and winter penalty), terrain and hilliness, elevation, roads, and rivers.
  • 3 reads disease frequency: how often diseases strike here per year, plus pollution and haze data if the Biotech DLC is active.
  • 4 reads time zone and global coordinates: the tile's latitude and longitude, and its UTC offset.
  • 5 reads regions and landmarks: the region or feature name, plus any landmarks (DLC only).

For how each biome plays and what a good starting climate looks like, see the Biomes article on the RimWorld wiki.

docs.title: Finding a site with the scanner
docs.text:
The scanner is the fastest way to locate anything on the map without arrowing across it. On the world map its categories include biomes, roads, and settlements. Switch categories with Ctrl+Page Up and Ctrl+Page Down, move between entries with Page Up and Page Down, and press Home to jump the cursor to the current entry.

When the scanner lands on a clump of related tiles (such as a biome spanning many tiles), it reports a tile count. Press Home once to jump to the nearest edge of the clump. If the clump has a distinct center, the mod offers a hint: press Home a second time to jump to the center.

To find neutral factions nearby, switch the scanner to the settlements category. The scanner announces each settlement's faction name and whether it is hostile or friendly.

For the full set of scanner keys, see The scanner.

docs.title: Where you can and cannot settle
docs.text:
• You cannot settle on a tile already owned by a faction. The game will refuse and explain why.
  • Settling within 5 tiles of another faction's settlement incurs a goodwill penalty for crowding them. Settle at least 5 tiles away to avoid it. There are no friendly factions to settle near at this stage: other factions are hostile or neutral.

If a tile is otherwise invalid (an ocean tile, for example), the game tells you when you try to settle.

docs.title: Settling
docs.text:
